Typical standard operating procedures are either to leverage software that performs a statistical analysis of time-dependent data to alarm, to make measurements (dosimetric or spectroscopic) at specific locations or intervals for subsequent analysis, or to make manual assessments of data collected through interpretation of the data shown in the sensor system’s user interface (UI). Alarms or anomalous measurements then cause the operator to perform additional actions, e.g., follow-on measurements to attribute the anomalous condition to surroundings, document the environment at the time of alarm, or alert others as a form of response. SDF automates much of the analysis and documentation process, easing operator burden. SDF also incorporates spatial information to account for multiple measurements of the same area, resulting in higher sensitivity to anomalies [1]. Use of imaging detector systems is another general application where the detector system is pointedattheregionofinterestanda‘dwell’measurementisconducteduntilsufficientstatisticsare obtained to create an image of the most probable location or distribution of radiological material within the field of view. In some scenarios, a second image is then collected from a different perspective to triangulate a source position through parallax. Because SDF enables imaging systems to be free-moving, operators can quickly identify higher activity areas and move the imager closer to those objects with spectroscopic characteristics of interest. This results in image creation in orders of magnitude shorter timescales and leverages multiple fields of view, providing depth resolution from a single collection resulting in a 3D radiological map, as opposed to the 2D projection generated by a single static, long-dwell measurements. Inlightoftheobservationthatthestate-of-the-artmeasurementtechniquesinducelogisticaland technical shortcomings in the case of some applications, researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) and Sandia National Laboratories (SNL), conducted a study of the NNSA- relevant missions and applications which the SDF technology, broadly, could impact; what R&D would be necessary to realize those beneficial mission impacts; and where there is intersecting and/or overlapping R&D, which may be most impactful overall. In the conduct of this scoping study, the authors conducted interviews with researchers and stakeholders across NNSA and held a workshop to present their preliminary findings to the NNSA community. The overall approach to this study was to first identify NNSA-relevant missions and potential applications of SDF within those missions and to then present those SDF applications to mission stakeholders and experts in the form of interviews, which consisted both of a presentation of the SDF technology and a follow-on discussion. During those discussions stakeholders often provided input that identified further applications of SDF and helped the study authors understand their perspectives on how both existing SDF capabilities and related improvements to the technology could impact their mission.
